title: Why Bleak Expectations didn’t live up to expectations- Theatre version of radio comedy reviewed
transcript: Hello and welcome to Theater Reviews with Paul 7 and I'm watching Bleak Expectations at the Criterion Theater. Whether you've read any Dickens or not, or whether you've heard the BBC Radio 4 comedy, Bleak Expectations or not, you'll find plenty to keep you amused in this sendup of Dickens novels and of Victorian values. By the way, if you enjoy my reviews, please like, comment, and subscribe. So to bleak expectations, if you're not familiar with the radio show, the nearest comparison I can give you is probably Black Adder. Mark Evans is a talented comedy writer who shares that series love of outlandish similes, anacronisms, and silly names, and he peppers the play with them. Well, actually, he could have been more liberal with this seasoning because what he's cooked up doesn't quite provide the feast of laughter you might expect. The jokes are fun, though. It was as if a giant teapot had poured sorrow upon the household and no one had said when or something like that. Or the twisting of famous Dickens phrases as when in response to some awful food. Please sir, may I have some less. And there's the familiar mocking of Victorian society. Familiar that is from pretty much every Victorian parody. You know, we do like to laugh smugly at uh the Victorians patronizing attitude to women and their prudy and uh their toxic masculinity. And this is good when concentrated into a halfhour episode. But when it's spread over two hours, it does begin to seem like lots of variations on the same few jokes. One difference from the radio show is of course visual humor. In fact, the show takes full advantage of the opportunity to introduce a great deal of physical comedy. Slapstick, gurning expressions, fighting, a jewel between the sword and the baguette is particularly funny, and lots of falling over and a French far amount of going in and out of doors. Caroline Leslie's slick direction ensures the visual element never flags. and Katy Leas's set, as well as being suitably Denzian, incorporates countless doors through which the far can flourish. The evening greatly benefits from having a celebrity guest playing Pip, uh, the narrator who tells us the story of his life. He's the author of many semi-autobiographical novels bearing a similarity to the works of Dickens, such as Massive Dorant. Each guest is engaged for a week, and you can look at the schedule to choose who you would like to see. Our story teller was Sally Phillips. Complete with mustache, deadpan delivery, knowing eyes, and the air of someone who'd rather not be there. She provided one of the highlights of the show. Not that the cast weren't good, too, as they took Pip and his cohorts through numerous trials and tribulations inspired by Mr. Dickens. From tragic childhood to horrific boarding school to having his fortune stolen in a court case to constantly losing people he loves. Dom Hudson makes a brighteyed and bushytailed hero. JJ Henry is his warm but dim friend Harry. Serena Mantagi plays his plucky sister Pipper. Rachel Summers is a young woman dripping with sexual frustration. Shane David Joseph and Ash Blackwood bounce around in many roles. John Hopkins is an excellent pantoime villain, while Mark Pickering made the most of the chance to play multiple members of the nasty hardthrer family, rolling his eyes and hamming it up for all he was worth. Like a Victorian railway train, the play chugs nicely down the track at first, but by the end the steam and the novelty begins to run out. I found I'd enjoyed my evening, but I was not thinking, "Please, sir, may I have some more." I hope you found this review uh useful and uh if you did, please like, comment, and subscribe so you'll be the first to know about my future reviews. And you can follow me on Twitter, Masterdan, Instagram, and Facebook. If you'd like to read my reviews, go to theater.reviews. reviews. Thank you for watching.
